content: This infection is caused by a fungal organism that was previously classified as Exophiala werneckii. However, it has been reclassified and is now known as Hortaea werneckii. Additionally, the causative organism has also been described under the name Phaeoannellomyces werneckii. The diagnosis of the fungal infection known as tinea nigra is established through microscopic examination of skin scrapings. These scrapings are mixed with potassium hydroxide (KOH), which serves to lyse non-fungal debris, allowing for clearer visualization of fungal elements. Tinea nigra is a condition that has been extensively documented and illustrated in dermatological atlases. These resources provide visual references to aid in the identification and understanding of the condition. Tinea nigra must be distinguished from other diseases that present with similar symptoms, such as erythematous, scaly, annular, and pruritic rashes. The differential diagnosis includes a range of conditions that may mimic the clinical appearance of tinea nigra. The treatment for tinea nigra involves the topical application of dandruff shampoo containing selenium sulfide to the affected skin. Alternatively, topical antifungal imidazoles, such as ketoconazole, may also be used. This treatment approach is similar to the management of other fungal infections, such as tinea versicolor or pityriasis versicolor.
